entries.da019c6ade5b0b38f213464d95d977a1a620300d: <div sID="gen2035" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="30" osisID="Exod.30" sID="Exod.30"/> <div eID="gen2035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2036" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2037" type="x-p"/> Moses is, in this chapter, further instructed, I. Concerning the altar of incense, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.1-Exod.30.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. II. Concerning the ransom-money which the Israelites were to pay, when they were numbered, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.11-Exod.30.16">ver. 11-16</reference>. III. Concerning the laver of brass, which was set for the priests to wash in, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.17-Exod.30.21">ver. 17-21</reference>. IV. Concerning the making up of the anointing oil, and the use of it, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.22-Exod.30.33">ver. 22-33</reference>. V. Concerning the incense and perfume which were to be burned on the golden altar, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.34">ver. 34</reference>, &c.
entries.25662f4d91a86cf750b68b359fd33ddcbda9cdb1: <div eID="gen2037" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2036" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Tabernacles and Its Furniture. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2038" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And thou shalt make an altar to burn incense upon: <hi type="italic">of</hi> shittim wood shalt thou make it. <hi type="super">2</hi> A cubit <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the length thereof, and a cubit the breadth thereof; foursquare shall it be: and two cubits <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the height thereof: the horns thereof <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> of the same. 3 And thou shalt overlay it with pure gold, the top thereof, and the sides thereof round about, and the horns thereof; and thou shalt make unto it a crown of gold round about. <hi type="super">4</hi> And two golden rings shalt thou make to it under the crown of it, by the two corners thereof, upon the two sides of it shalt thou make <hi type="italic">it;</hi> and they shall be for places for the staves to bear it withal. <hi type="super">5</hi> And thou shalt make the staves <hi type="italic">of</hi> shittim wood, and overlay them with gold. <hi type="super">6</hi> And thou shalt put it before the vail that <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat that <hi type="italic">is</hi> over the testimony, where I will meet with thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Aaron shall burn thereon sweet incense every morning: when he dresseth the lamps, he shall burn incense upon it. <hi type="super">8</hi> And when Aaron lighteth the lamps at even, he shall burn incense upon it, a perpetual incense before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> throughout your generations. <hi type="super">9</hi> Ye shall offer no strange incense thereon, nor burnt sacrifice, nor meat offering; neither shall ye pour drink offering thereon. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Aaron shall make an atonement upon the horns of it once in a year with the blood of the sin offering of atonements: once in the year shall he make atonement upon it throughout your generations: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> most holy unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen2038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2039" type="x-p"/> I. The orders given concerning the altar of incense are, 1. That it was to be made of wood, and covered with gold, pure gold, about a yard high and half a yard square, with horns at the corners, a golden cornice round it, with rings and staves of gold, for the convenience of carrying it, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.1-Exod.30.5">v. 1-5</reference>. It does not appear that there was any grate to this altar for the ashes to fall into, that they might be taken away; but, when they burnt incense, a golden censer was brought with coals in it, and placed upon the altar, and in that censer the incense was burnt, and with it all the coals were taken away, so that no coals nor ashes fell upon the altar. The measure of the altar of incense in Ezekiel's temple is double to what it is here (<reference osisRef="Ezek.41.22">Ezek. xli. 22</reference>), and it is there called <hi type="italic">an altar of wood,</hi> and there is no mention of gold, to signify that the incense, in gospel times, should be spiritual, the worship plain, and the service of God enlarged, for <hi type="italic">in every place incense should be offered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.1.11">Mal. i. 11</reference>. 2. That it was to be placed before the veil, on the outside of that partition, but before the mercy-seat, which was within the veil, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.6">v. 6</reference>. For though he that ministered at the altar could not see the mercy-seat, the veil interposing, yet he must look towards it, and direct his incense that way, to teach us that though we cannot with our bodily eyes see the throne of grace, that blessed mercy-seat (for it is such a throne of glory that God, in compassion to us, holds back the face of it, and spreads a cloud upon it), yet we must in prayer by faith set ourselves before it, direct our prayer, and look up. 3. That Aaron was to burn sweet incense upon this altar, every morning and every evening, about half a pound at a time, which was intended, not only to take away the ill smell of the flesh that was burnt daily on the brazen altar, but for the honour of God, and to show the acceptableness of his people's services to him, and the pleasure which they should take in ministering to him, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.7-Exod.30.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. As by the offerings on the brazen altar satisfaction was made for what had been done displeasing to God, so, by the offering on this, what they did well was, as it were, recommended to the divine acceptance; for our two great concerns with God are to be acquitted from guilt and accepted as righteous in his sight. 4. That nothing was to be offered upon it but incense, nor any incense but that which was appointed, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.9">v. 9</reference>. God will have his own service done according to his own appointment, and not otherwise. 5. That this altar should be purified with the blood of the sin-offering put upon the <hi type="italic">horns of it,</hi> every year, upon <hi type="italic">the day of atonement,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.30.10">v. 10</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Lev.16.18-Lev.16.19">Lev. xvi. 18, 19</reference>. The high priest was to take this in his way, as he came out from the holy of holies. This was to intimate to them that the sins of the priests who ministered at this altar, and of the people for whom they ministered, put a ceremonial impurity upon it, from which it must be cleansed by the blood of atonement. <div eID="gen2039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2040" type="x-p"/> II. This incense-altar typified, 1. The mediation of Christ. The brazen altar in the court was a type of Christ dying on earth; the golden altar in the sanctuary was a type of Christ interceding in heaven, in virtue of his satisfaction. This altar was before the mercy-seat; for Christ always appears in the presence of God for us; he is our <hi type="italic">advocate with the father</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1 John ii. 1</reference>), and his intercession is unto God of a sweet-smelling savour. This altar had a crown fixed to it; for Christ intercedes as king. <hi type="italic">Father, I will,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.24">John xvii. 24</reference>. 2. The devotions of the saints, whose prayers are said to be set forth before God as incense, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Ps. cxli. 2</reference>. As the smoke of the incense ascended, so much our desires towards God rise in prayer, being kindled with the fire of holy love and other pious affections. When the priest was burning incense the people were praying (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.10">Luke i. 10</reference>), to signify that prayer is the true incense. This incense was offered daily, it was a perpetual incense (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.8">v. 8</reference>); for we must pray always, that is, we must keep up stated times for prayer every day, morning and evening, at least, and never omit it, but thus pray without ceasing. The lamps were dressed or lighted at the same time that the incense was burnt, to teach us that the reading of the scriptures (which are our light and lamp) is a part of our daily work, and should ordinarily accompany our prayers and praises. When we speak to God we must hear what God says to us, and thus the communion is complete. The devotions of sanctified souls are well-pleasing to God, of a sweet-smelling savour; the prayers of saints are compared to sweet odours (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.8">Rev. v. 8</reference>), but it is the incense which Christ adds to them that makes them acceptable (<reference osisRef="Rev.8.3">Rev. viii. 3</reference>), and his blood that atones for the guilt which cleaves to our best services. And, if the heart and life be not holy, even <hi type="italic">incense is an abomination</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa. i. 13</reference>), and he that offers it is <hi type="italic">as if he blessed an idol,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.56.3">Isa. lxvi. 3</reference>.
entries.012d8ca0702ae4ddc68dc950556ffa52d1c73920: <div eID="gen2040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2041" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">12</hi> When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when <hi type="italic">thou</hi> numberest them. <hi type="super">13</hi> This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel <hi type="italic">is</hi> twenty gerahs:) an half shekel <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the offering of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> Every one that passeth among them that are numbered, from twenty years old and above, shall give an offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel, when <hi type="italic">they</hi> give an offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to make an atonement for your souls. 16 And thou shalt take the atonement money of the children of Israel, and shalt appoint it for the service of the tabernacle of the congregation; that it may be a memorial unto the children of Israel before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to make an atonement for your souls. <div eID="gen2041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2042" type="x-p"/> Some observe that the repetition of those words, <hi type="italic">The Lord spoke unto Moses,</hi> here and afterwards (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.17">v. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.22">22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.34">34</reference>), intimates that God did not deliver these precepts to Moses in the mount, in a continued discourse, but with many intermissions, giving him time either to write what was said to him or at least to charge his memory with it. Christ gave instructions to his disciples as they were able to hear them. Moses is here ordered to levy money upon the people by way of poll, so much a head, for the service of the tabernacle. This he must do when he numbered the people. Some think that it refers only to the first numbering of them, now when the tabernacle was set up; and that this tax was to make up what was deficient in the voluntary contributions for the finishing of the work, or rather for the beginning of the service in the tabernacle. Others think that it was afterwards repeated upon any emergency and always when the people were numbered, and that David offended in not demanding it when he numbered the people. But many of the Jewish writers, and others from them, are of opinion that it was to be an annual tribute, only it was begun when Moses first numbered the people. This was that tribute-money which Christ paid, for fear of offending his adversaries (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.27">Matt. xvii. 27</reference>), when yet he showed good reason why he should have been excused. Men were appointed in every city to receive this payment yearly. Now, 1. The tribute to be paid was <hi type="italic">half a shekel,</hi> about fifteen pence of our money. The rich were not to give more, nor the poor less (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.15">v. 15</reference>), to intimate that the souls of the rich and poor are alike precious, and that God is <hi type="italic">no respecter of persons,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.34">Acts x. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.19">Job xxxiv. 19</reference>. In other offerings men were to give according to their ability; but this, which was the <hi type="italic">ransom of the soul,</hi> must be alike for all; for the rich have as much need of Christ as the poor, and the poor are as welcome to him as the rich. They both alike contributed to the maintenance of the temple-service, because both were to have a like interest in it and benefit by it. In Christ and his ordinances <hi type="italic">rich and poor meet together; the Lord is the Maker,</hi> the Lord Christ is the Redeemer of them both, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.2">Prov. xxii. 2</reference>. The Jews say, "If a man refused to pay this tribute, he was not comprehended in the expiation." 2. this tribute was to be paid as a <hi type="italic">ransom of the soul, that there might be no plague among them.</hi> Hereby they acknowledged that they received their lives from God, that they had forfeited their lives to him, and that they depended upon his power and patience for the continuance of them; and thus they did homage to the God of their lives, and deprecated those plagues which their sins had deserved. 3. This money that was raised was to be employed in the service of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.16">v. 16</reference>); with it they bought sacrifices, flour, incense, wine, oil, fuel, salt, priests' garments, and all other things which the whole congregation was interested in. Note, Those that have the benefit of God's tabernacle among them must be willing to defray the expenses of it, and not grudge the necessary charges of God's public worship. Thus we must honour the Lord with our substance, and reckon that best laid out which is laid out in the service of God. Money indeed cannot make an <hi type="italic">atonement for the soul,</hi> but it may be used for the honour of him who has made the atonement, and for the maintenance of the gospel by which the atonement is applied.
entries.14fd1285fc1344fa8ccbdf9be201e1c450c84c52: <div eID="gen2042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2043" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">18</hi> Thou shalt also make a laver <hi type="italic">of</hi> brass, and his foot <hi type="italic">also of</hi> brass, to wash <hi type="italic">withal:</hi> and thou shalt put it between the tabernacle of the congregation and the altar, and thou shalt put water therein. 19 For Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet thereat: <hi type="super">20</hi> When they go into the tabernacle of the congregation, they shall wash with water, that they die not; or when they come near to the altar to minister, to burn offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">21</hi> So they shall wash their hands and their feet, that they die not: and it shall be a statute for ever to them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to him and to his seed throughout their generations. <div eID="gen2043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2044" type="x-p"/> Orders are here given, 1. For the making of a laver, or font, of brass, a large vessel, that would contain a good quantity of water, which was to be set near the door of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.18">v. 18</reference>. The foot of brass, it is supposed, was so contrived as to receive the water, which was let into it out of the laver by spouts or cocks. They then had a laver for the priests only to wash in, but to us now there is a fountain open for Judah and Jerusalem to wash in (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zech. xiii. 1</reference>), an inexhaustible <hi type="italic">fountain of living water,</hi> so that it is our own fault if we remain in our pollution. 2. For the using of this laver. Aaron and his sons must wash their hands and feet at this laver every time they went in to minister, every morning, at least, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.19-Exod.30.21">v. 19-21</reference>. For this purpose clean water was put into the laver fresh every day. Though they washed themselves ever so clean at their own houses, that would not serve; they must wash at the laver, because that was appointed for washing, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.12-2Kgs.5.14">2 Kings v. 12-14</reference>. This was designed, (1.) To teach them purity in all their ministrations, and to possess them with a reverence of God's holiness and a dread of the pollutions of sin. They must not only wash and be made clean when they were first consecrated, but they must wash and be kept clean whenever they went in to minister. He only shall <hi type="italic">stand in God's holy place</hi> that has <hi type="italic">clean hands and a pure heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.24.3-Ps.24.4">Ps. xxiv. 3, 4</reference>. And, (2.) It was to teach us, who are daily to attend upon God, daily to renew our repentance for sin and our believing application of the blood of Christ to our souls for remission; for in many things we daily offend and contract pollution, <reference osisRef="John.13.8 John.13.10">John xiii. 8, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.3.2">Jam. iii. 2</reference>. This is the preparation we are to make for solemn ordinances. <hi type="italic">Cleanse your hands and purify your hearts,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">draw nigh to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.4.8">Jam. iv. 8</reference>. To this law David alludes in <reference osisRef="Ps.26.6">Ps. xxvi. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will wash my hands in innocency, so will I compass thine altar, O Lord.</hi>
entries.f374cd7453f224b72f936ec3ab8a33e8fef8f278: <div eID="gen2044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2045" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Moreover the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">23</hi> Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred <hi type="italic">shekels,</hi> and of sweet cinnamon half so much, <hi type="italic">even</hi> two hundred and fifty <hi type="italic">shekels,</hi> and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty <hi type="italic">shekels,</hi> <hi type="super">24</hi> And of cassia five hundred <hi type="italic">shekels,</hi> after the shekel of the sanctuary, and of oil olive an hin: <hi type="super">25</hi> And thou shalt make it an oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary: it shall be an holy anointing oil. <hi type="super">26</hi> And thou shalt anoint the tabernacle of the congregation therewith, and the ark of the testimony, <hi type="super">27</hi> And the table and all his vessels, and the candlestick and his vessels, and the altar of incense, <hi type="super">28</hi> And the altar of burnt offering with all his vessels, and the laver and his foot. <hi type="super">29</hi> And thou shalt sanctify them, that they may be most holy: whatsoever toucheth them shall be holy. <hi type="super">30</hi> And thou shalt anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, that <hi type="italic">they</hi> may minister unto me in the priest's office. <hi type="super">31</hi> And thou shalt speak unto the children of Israel, saying, This shall be an holy anointing oil unto me throughout your generations. 32 Upon man's flesh shall it not be poured, neither shall ye make <hi type="italic">any other</hi> like it, after the composition of it: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> holy, <hi type="italic">and</hi> it shall be holy unto you. <hi type="super">33</hi> Whosoever compoundeth <hi type="italic">any</hi> like it, or whosoever putteth <hi type="italic">any</hi> of it upon a stranger, shall even be cut off from his people. <hi type="super">34</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Take unto thee sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum; <hi type="italic">these</hi> sweet spices with pure frankincense: of each shall there be a like <hi type="italic">weight:</hi> <hi type="super">35</hi> And thou shalt make it a perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together, pure <hi type="italic">and</hi> holy: <hi type="super">36</hi> And thou shalt beat <hi type="italic">some</hi> of it very small, and put of it before the testimony in the tabernacle of the congregation, where I will meet with thee: it shall be unto you most holy. <hi type="super">37</hi> And <hi type="italic">as for</hi> the perfume which thou shalt make, ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof: it shall be unto thee holy for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">38</hi> Whosoever shall make like unto that, to smell thereto, shall even be cut off from his people. <div eID="gen2045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2046" type="x-p"/> Directions are here given for the composition of the holy anointing oil and the incense that were to be used in the service of the tabernacle; with these God was to be honoured, and therefore he would appoint the making of them; for nothing comes <hi type="italic">to</hi> God but what comes <hi type="italic">from</hi> him. 1. The holy anointing oil is here ordered to be made up the ingredients, and their quantities, are prescribed, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.23-Exod.30.25">v. 23-25</reference>. Interpreters are not agreed concerning them; we are sure, in general, they were the best and fittest for the purpose; they must needs be so when the divine wisdom appointed them for the divine honour. It was to be compounded <hi type="italic">secundum artem—after the art of the apothecary</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.25">v. 25</reference>); the spices, which were in all nearly half a hundred weight, were to be infused in the oil, which was to be about five or six quarts, and then strained out, leaving an admirable sweet smell in the oil. With this oil God's tent and all the furniture of it were to be anointed; it was to be used also in the consecration of the priests, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.26-Exod.30.30">v. 26-30</reference>. It was to be continued <hi type="italic">throughout their generations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.30.31">v. 31</reference>. The tradition of the Jews is that this very oil which was prepared by Moses himself lasted till near the captivity. But bishop Patrick shows the great improbability of the tradition, and supposes that it was repeated according to the prescription here, for Solomon was anointed with it (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.39">2 Kings i. 39</reference>), and some other of the kings; and all the high priests with such a quantity of it that it ran down to the skirts of the garments; and we read of the making up of this ointment (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.30">1 Chron. ix. 30</reference>): yet all agree that in the second temple there was none of this holy oil, which he supposes was owing to a notion they had that it was not lawful to make it up, Providence overruling that want as a presage of the better unction of the Holy Ghost in gospel times, the variety of whose gifts was typified by these several sweet ingredients. To show the excellency of holiness, there was that in the tabernacle which was in the highest degree grateful both to the sight and to the smell. Christ's name is said to be as <hi type="italic">ointment poured forth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.1.3">Cant. i. 3</reference>), and the good name of Christians better than <hi type="italic">precious ointment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Eccl. vii. 1</reference>. 2. The incense which was burned upon the golden altar was prepared of sweet spices likewise, though not so rare and rich as those of which the anointing oil was compounded, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.34-Exod.30.35">v. 34, 35</reference>. This was prepared once a year (the Jews say), a pound for each day of the year, and three pounds over for the day of atonement. When it was used, it was to be beaten very small: thus it pleased the Lord to bruise the Redeemer when he offered himself for a sacrifice of a sweet-smelling savour. 3. Concerning both these preparations the same law is here given (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.32-Exod.30.33">v. 32, 33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.37">37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.38">38</reference>), that the like should not be made for any common use. Thus God would preserve in the people's minds a reverence for his own institutions, and teach us not to profane nor abuse any thing whereby God makes himself known, as those did who invented to themselves (for their common entertainments) instruments of music like David, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.5">Amos vi. 5</reference>. It is a great affront to God to jest with sacred things, particularly to make sport with the word and ordinances of God, or to treat them with lightness, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.5">Matt. xxii. 5</reference>. That which is God's peculiar must not be used as a common thing.  <chapter eID="Exod.30"/> <div eID="gen2046" type="x-p"/>

entries.1714d25b0d048f05bc186b8403e4479874db5cc0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv891"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 30</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.30.1-Exod.30.38">Ex 30:1-38</reference>. The Altar of Incense.</title> <div sID="gen1236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv891"/><hi type="bold">1. thou shalt make an altar to burn incense upon, &c.--</hi>Its material was to be like that of the ark of the testimony, but its dimensions very small [Ex 25:10]. <div eID="gen1236" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d5f494786f2e7fb628f66c31142d92cadbec639: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv892"/><div sID="gen1237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv892"/><hi type="bold">2-4. foursquare--</hi>the meaning of which is not that it was to be entirely of a cubical form, but that upon its upper and under surface, it showed four equal sides. It was twice as high as it was broad, being twenty-one inches broad and three feet six inches high. It had "horns"; its top or flat surface was surmounted by an ornamental ledge or rim, called a crown, and it was furnished at the sides with rings for carriage. Its only accompanying piece of furniture was a golden censer or pan, in which the incense was set fire to upon the altar. Hence it was called the altar of incense, or the "golden altar" [Ex 39:38; 40:26], from the profuse degree in which it was gilded or overlaid with the precious metal. This splendor was adapted to the early age of the church, but in later times, when the worship was to be more spiritual, the altar of incense is prophetically described as not of gold but of wood, and double the size of that in the tabernacle, because the church should be vastly extended (Mal 1:11). <div eID="gen1237" type="x-p"/>
entries.43c081bce1797d7ca72f0752fcc8c05410825b48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv893"/><div sID="gen1238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv893"/><hi type="bold">6. thou shalt put it before the veil that is by the ark of the testimony--</hi>which separated the holy from the most holy place. The altar was in the middle between the table of showbread and the candlestick next the holy of holies, at equal distances from the north and south walls; in other words, it occupied a spot on the outside of the great partition veil, but directly in front of the mercy seat, which was within that sacred enclosure; so that although the priest who ministered at this altar could not behold the mercy seat, he was to look towards it, and present his incense in that direction. This was a special arrangement, and it was designed to teach the important lesson that, though we cannot with the eye of sense, see the throne of grace, we must "direct our prayer to it and look up" [Psa 5:3] (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">2Co 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.20">He 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.4.1">Re 4:1</reference>). <div eID="gen1238" type="x-p"/>
entries.60cd088b15a48ae23ce3731c67711a2fe010887c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv894"/><div sID="gen1239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv894"/><hi type="bold">7-8. Aaron shall burn thereon sweet incense--</hi>literally, "incense of spices"--Strong aromatic substances were burnt upon this altar to counteract by their odoriferous fragrance the offensive fumes of the sacrifices; or the incense was employed in an offering of tributary homage which the Orientals used to make as a mark of honor to kings; and as God was Theocratic Ruler of Israel, His palace was not to be wanting in a usage of such significancy. Both these ends were served by this altar--that of fumigating the apartments of the sacred edifice, while the pure lambent flame, according to Oriental notions, was an honorary tribute to the majesty of Israel's King. But there was a far higher meaning in it still; for as the tabernacle was not only a palace for Israel's King, but a place of worship for Israel's God, this altar was immediately connected with a religious purpose. In the style of the sacred writers, incense was a symbol or emblem of prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.8">Re 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.3">8:3</reference>). From the uniform combination of the two services, it is evident that the incense was an emblem of the prayers of sincere worshippers ascending to heaven in the cloud of perfume; and, accordingly, the priest who officiated at this altar typified the intercessory office of Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.10">Lu 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.7.25">He 7:25</reference>).<div eID="gen1239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every morning ... at even--</hi>In every period of the national history this daily worship was scrupulously observed. <div eID="gen1240" type="x-p"/>
entries.f157df8655a1bc797d17455eb4b55b66d315b4c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv896"/><div sID="gen1242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv896"/><hi type="bold">9. Ye shall offer no strange incense--</hi>that is, of a different composition from that of which the ingredients are described so minutely. <div eID="gen1242" type="x-p"/>
entries.853094eabc42cd953a2cae0b6e92654af33a8267: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv897"/><div sID="gen1243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv897"/><hi type="bold">11-16. When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel, &c.--</hi>Moses did so twice, and doubtless observed the law here prescribed. The tax was not levied from women, minors, old men (<reference osisRef="Num.1.42">Nu 1:42</reference>, 45), and the Levites (<reference osisRef="Num.1.47">Nu 1:47</reference>), they being not numbered. Assuming the shekel of the sanctuary to be about half an ounce troy, though nothing certain is known about it, the sum payable by each individual was two and four pence. This was not a voluntary contribution, but a ransom for the soul or lives of the people. It was required from all classes alike, and a refusal to pay implied a wilful exclusion from the privileges of the sanctuary, as well as exposure to divine judgments. It was probably the same impost that was exacted from our Lord (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.24-Matt.17.27">Mt 17:24-27</reference>), and it was usually devoted to repairs and other purposes connected with the services of the sanctuary. <div eID="gen1243" type="x-p"/>
entries.531be1bc0806ffad6cb865118d83ade39c242821: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv898"/><div sID="gen1244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv898"/><hi type="bold">18-21. Thou shalt ... make a laver of brass--</hi>Though not actually forming a component part of the furniture of the tabernacle, this vase was closely connected with it; and though from standing at the entrance it would be a familiar object, it possessed great interest and importance from the baptismal purposes to which it was applied. No data are given by which its form and size can be ascertained; but it was probably a miniature pattern of Solomon's--a circular basin.<div eID="gen1244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his foot--</hi>supposed not to be the pedestal on which it rested, but a trough or shallow receptacle below, into which the water, let out from a cock or spout, flowed; for the way in which all Eastern people wash their hands or feet is by pouring upon them the water which falls into a basin. This laver was provided for the priests alone. But in the Christian dispensation, all believers are priests, and hence the apostle exhorts them how to draw near to God (<reference osisRef="John.13.10">Joh 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">He 10:22</reference>). <div eID="gen1245" type="x-p"/>
entries.73004652c7a67ca29a85d38936ee9b6c0c09e4cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv899"/><div sID="gen1246" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv899"/><hi type="bold">23-33. Take thou also ... principal spices, &c.--</hi>Oil is frequently mentioned in Scripture as an emblem of sanctification, and anointing with it a means of designating objects as well as persons to the service of God. Here it is prescribed by divine authority, and the various ingredients in their several proportions described which were to compose the oil used in consecrating the furniture of the tabernacle.<div eID="gen1246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">myrrh--</hi>a fragrant and medicinal gum from a little known tree in Arabia.<div eID="gen1247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sweet cinnamon--</hi>produced from a species of laurel or sweet bay, found chiefly in Ceylon, growing to a height of twenty feet: this spice is extracted from the inner bark, but it is not certain whether that mentioned by Moses is the same as that with which we are familiar.<div eID="gen1248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sweet calamus--</hi>or sweet cane, a product of Arabia and India, of a tawny color in appearance; it is like the common cane and strongly odoriferous. <div eID="gen1249" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b734c4c4aa016528dc706bd3d54a5e9d89712c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv901"/><div sID="gen1252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv901"/><hi type="bold">34-38. the Lord said unto Moses, Take unto thee sweet spices--</hi>These were:<div eID="gen1252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stacte--</hi>the finest myrrh;<div eID="gen1253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">onycha--</hi>supposed to be an odoriferous shell;<div eID="gen1254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">galbanum--</hi>a gum resin from an umbelliferous plant.<div eID="gen1255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">frankincense--</hi>a dry, resinous, aromatic gum, of a yellow color, which comes from a tree in Arabia, and is obtained by incision of the bark. This incense was placed within the sanctuary, to be at hand when the priest required to burn on the altar. The art of compounding unguents and perfumes was well known in Egypt, where sweet-scented spices were extensively used not only in common life, but in the ritual of the temples. Most of the ingredients here mentioned have been found on minute examination of mummies and other Egyptian relics; and the Israelites, therefore, would have the best opportunities of acquiring in that country the skill in pounding and mixing them which they were called to exercise in the service of the tabernacle. But the recipe for the incense as well as for the oil in the tabernacle, though it receives illustration from the customs of Egypt, was peculiar, and being prescribed by divine authority, was to be applied to no common or inferior purpose. <chapter eID="Exod.30"/>

entries.f0bbeb6127789337f41d18a3eb48c7d5066316e4: <div eID="gen3864" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen3865" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3866" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3866" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3865" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3867" type="x-p"/> The altar of burnt incense, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.1">Exo 30:1</reference>. Dimensions, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.2">Exo 30:2</reference>. Golden crown, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.3">Exo 30:3</reference>. Rings and staves, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.4">Exo 30:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.5">Exo 30:5</reference>. Where placed, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.6">Exo 30:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.7">Exo 30:7</reference>. Use, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.8-Exo.30.10">Exo 30:8-10</reference>. The ransom price of half a shekel, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.11-Exo.30.13">Exo 30:11-13</reference>. Who were to pay it, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.14">Exo 30:14</reference>. The rich and the poor to pay alike, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.15">Exo 30:15</reference>. The use to which it was applied, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.16">Exo 30:16</reference>. The brazen laver, and its uses, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.17-Exo.30.21">Exo 30:17-21</reference>. The holy anointing oil, and its component parts, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.22-Exo.30.25">Exo 30:22-25</reference>. To be applied to the tabernacle, ark, golden table, candlestick, altar of burnt-offerings, and the laver, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.26-Exo.30.29">Exo 30:26-29</reference>. And to Aaron and his sons, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.30">Exo 30:30</reference>. Never to be applied to any other uses, and none like it ever to be made, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.31-Exo.30.33">Exo 30:31-33</reference>. The perfume, and how made, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.34">Exo 30:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.35">Exo 30:35</reference>. Its use, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.36">Exo 30:36</reference>. Nothing similar to it ever to be made, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.37">Exo 30:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.38">Exo 30:38</reference>. <div eID="gen3867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3868" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen3868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3869" type="x-p"/> Altar to burn incense - The Samaritan omits the ten first verses of this chapter, because it inserts them after <reference osisRef="Exo.26.32">Exo 26:32</reference> (note). <div eID="gen3869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3870" type="x-p"/> Shittim wood - The same of which the preceding articles were made, because it was abundant in those parts, and because it was very durable; hence everywhere the Septuagint translation, which was made in Egypt, renders the original by ξυλον ασηπτον, incorruptible wood.
entries.b2d8edf1f199f486981382186650f5c2752b21d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen3870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3871" type="x-p"/> Four-square - That is, on the upper or under surface, as it showed four equal sides; but it was twice as high as it was broad, being twenty-one inches broad, and three feet six inches high. It was called, not only the altar of incense, but also the golden altar, <reference osisRef="Num.4.11">Num 4:11</reference>. For the crown, horns, staves, etc., see on the altar of burnt-offering, <reference osisRef="Exo.27.1">Exo 27:1</reference> (note), etc.
entries.4ad5cf65306e48ff82a4fdff07aa15cfd30ee798: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen3871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3872" type="x-p"/> Before the mercy-seat that is over the testimony - These words in the original are supposed to be a repetition, by mistake, of the preceding clause; the word הפרכת happarocheth, the veil, being corrupted by interchanging two letters into הכפרת haccapporeth, the mercy-seat; and this, as Dr. Kennicott observes, places the altar of incense before the mercy-seat, and consequently In the holy of holies! Now this could not be, as the altar of incense was attended every day, and the holy of holies entered only once in the year. The five words which appear to be a repetition are wanting in twenty-six of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., and in the Samaritan. The verse reads better without them, and is more consistent with the rest of the account.
entries.7eb90ca72f1b5a4d04240836554abd3be22514c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen3872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3873" type="x-p"/> When he dresseth the lamps - Prepares the wicks, and puts in fresh oil for the evening. <div eID="gen3873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3874" type="x-p"/> Shall burn incense upon it - Where so many sacrifices were offered it was essentially necessary to have some pleasing perfume to counteract the disagreeable smells that must have arisen from the slaughter of so many animals, the sprinkling of so much blood, and the burning of so much flesh, etc. The perfume that was to be burnt on this altar is described <reference osisRef="Exo.30.34">Exo 30:34</reference>. No blood was ever sprinkled on this altar, except on the day of general expiation, which happened only once in the year, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.10">Exo 30:10</reference>. But the perfume was necessary in every part of the tabernacle and its environs.
entries.e8b8ad9373954733564750e110b2fc6cc57f6717: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen3874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3875" type="x-p"/> No strange incense - None made in any other way. <div eID="gen3875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3876" type="x-p"/> Nor burnt-sacrifice - It should be an altar for incense, and for no other use.
entries.ff42e85daa2b8e7bc2767626e04abb1b47f753ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen3876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3877" type="x-p"/> An atonement - once in a year - On the tenth day of the seventh month. See <reference osisRef="Lev.16.18">Lev 16:18</reference> (note), etc., and the notes there. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Lev.16.21">Lev 16:21</reference> (note), etc.
entries.640e9eda363dc982cc2e4ee5e2b79a27e65d2db5: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen3877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3878" type="x-p"/> Then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul - This was a very important ordinance, and should be seriously considered. See <reference osisRef="Exo.30.13">Exo 30:13</reference> (note).
entries.0b87c7c34844bc8b1165f8e4b4e3234237b80368: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen3878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3879" type="x-p"/> Half a shekel - Each of the Israelites was ordered to give as a ransom for his soul (i.e., for his life) half a shekel, according to the shekel of the sanctuary. From this we may learn, <div eID="gen3879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3880" type="x-p"/> 1. That the life of every man was considered as being forfeited to Divine justice. <div eID="gen3880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3881" type="x-p"/> 2. That the redemption money given, which was doubtless used in the service of the sanctuary, was ultimately devoted to the use and profit of those who gave it. <div eID="gen3881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3882" type="x-p"/> 3. That the standard by which the value of coin was ascertained, was kept in the sanctuary; for this appears to be the meaning of the words, after the shekel of the sanctuary. <div eID="gen3882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3883" type="x-p"/> 4. The shekel is here said to be twenty gerahs. A gerah, according to Maimonides, weighed sixteen barleycorns, a shekel three hundred and twenty of pure silver. The shekel is generally considered to be equal in value to three shillings English; the redemption money, therefore, must be about one shilling and sixpence. <div eID="gen3883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3884" type="x-p"/> 5. The rich were not to give more, the poor not to give less; to signify that all souls were equally precious in the sight of God, and that no difference of outward circumstances could affect the state of the soul; all had sinned, and all must be redeemed by the same price. <div eID="gen3884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3885" type="x-p"/> 6. This atonement must be made that there might be no plague among them, intimating that a plague or curse from God must light on those souls for whom the atonement was not made. <div eID="gen3885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3886" type="x-p"/> 7. This was to be a memorial unto the children of Israel, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.16">Exo 30:16</reference>, to bring to their remembrance their past deliverance, and to keep in view their future redemption. <div eID="gen3886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3887" type="x-p"/> 8. St. Peter seems to allude to this, and to intimate that this mode of atonement was ineffectual in itself, and only pointed out the great sacrifice which, in the fullness of time, should be made for the sin of the world. "Ye know," says he, "that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot: who verily was foreordained before the foundation of the world," etc.; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pet 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.19">1Pet 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.20">1Pet 1:20</reference>. <div eID="gen3887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3888" type="x-p"/> 9. Therefore all these things seem to refer to Christ alone, and to the atonement made by his blood; and upon him who is not interested in this atonement, God's plagues must be expected to fall. <div eID="gen3888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3889" type="x-p"/> Reader, acquaint now thyself with God and be at peace, and thereby good shall come unto thee.
entries.bee7ce63dabd356c87bdf080cbde93a685b055b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen3889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3890" type="x-p"/> A laver of brass - כיור kiyor sometimes signifies a caldron, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.14">1Sam 2:14</reference>; but it seems to signify any large round vessel or basin used for washing the hands and feet. There were doubtless cocks or spigots in it to draw off the water, as it is not likely the feet were put into it in order to be washed. The foot of the laver must mean the pedestal on which it stood.
entries.6fa9173ef1cd7d56158621e971e83a1581a2e812: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen3890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3891" type="x-p"/> They shall wash with water, that they die not - This was certainly an emblematical washing; and as the hands and the feet are particularly mentioned, it must refer to the purity of their whole conduct. Their hands - all their works, their feet - all their goings, must be washed - must be holiness unto the Lord. And this washing must be repeated every time they entered into the tabernacle, or when they came near to the altar to minister. This washing was needful because the priests all ministered barefoot; but it was equally so because of the guilt they might have contracted, for the washing was emblematical of the putting away of sin, or what St. Paul calls the laver of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Ghost, (<reference osisRef="Tit.3.5">Tit 3:5</reference>), as the influences of the Spirit must be repeated for the purification of the soul, as frequently as any moral defilement has been contracted.
entries.ec13c7efb7bb3b85f86dd7ff81c98435724b1e02: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen3891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3892" type="x-p"/> And it shall be a statute for ever - To continue, in its literal meaning, as long as the Jewish economy lasted, and, in its spiritual meaning, to the end of time. What an important lesson does this teach the ministers of the Gospel of Christ! Each time they minister in public, whether in dispensing the Word or the Sacraments, they should take heed that they have a fresh application of the grace and spirit of Christ, to do away past transgressions or unfaithfulness, and to enable them to minister with the greater effect, as being in the Divine favor, and consequently entitled to expect all the necessary assistances of the Divine unction, to make their ministrations spirit and life to the people. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.20">Exo 29:20</reference>.
entries.853186cffa121b3add6db48c251a77a0629d18e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen3892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3893" type="x-p"/> Take - unto thee principal spices - From this and the following verse we learn that the holy anointing oil was compounded of the following ingredients: - <div eID="gen3893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3894" type="x-p"/> Pure myrrh, מר דרור mar deror, 500 shekels <div eID="gen3894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3895" type="x-p"/> Sweet cinnamon, קנמן בשם kinnemon besem, 250 shekels. (probably from Arabia) <div eID="gen3895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3896" type="x-p"/> Sweet calamus, קנה בשם keneh bosem, or sweet 250 shekels. cane, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">Jer 6:20</reference> - Calamus aromaticus. <div eID="gen3896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3897" type="x-p"/> Cassia, קדה kiddah, (cassia lignea), brought 500 shekels. Also from Arabia. <div eID="gen3897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3898" type="x-p"/> Olive oil, שמן זית shemen sayith, one hin, about 5 quarts. <div eID="gen3898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3899" type="x-p"/> Myrrh is the produce of an oriental tree not well known, and is collected by making an incision in the tree. What is now called by this name is precisely the same with that of the ancients. 500 shekels of the first and last, make 48 lbs. 4 oz. 12 dwts. 21 21/31 grs. 250 of the cinnamon and calamus. 24 lbs. 2 oz. 6 dwts.10 26/31 grs. <div eID="gen3899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3900" type="x-p"/> Olive oil is supposed to be the best preservative of odours. <div eID="gen3900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3901" type="x-p"/> As the gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit are termed the anointing of the Holy Ghost, therefore this holy ointment appears to have been designed as emblematical of those gifts and graces. See <reference osisRef="Act.1.5">Act 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.10.38">Act 10:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.21">2Cor 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Jn.2.20">1Jn 2:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.2.27">1Jn 2:27</reference>.
entries.51f8eb92362e111f5212aba7d4222ffb96129404: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen3901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3902" type="x-p"/> After the art of the apothecary - The original, רקח rokeach, signifies a compounder or confectioner; any person who compounds drugs, aromatics, etc.
entries.9494311b6969488669d21bd42eed99523a9c7190: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen3902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3903" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt anoint Aaron and his sons - For the reason of this anointing, see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.7">Exo 29:7</reference>. It seems that this anointing oil was an emblem of Divine teaching, and especially of those influences by which the Church of Christ was, in the beginning, guided into all truth; as is evident from the allusion to it by St. John: "Ye have an unction from the Holy One, and ye know all things. The anointing which ye have received from him abideth in you, and ye need not that any man teach you; but as the same anointing teacheth you of all things, and is truth, and is no lie, and even as it hath taught you, ye shall abide in Him; <reference osisRef="1Jn.2.20">1Jn 2:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.2.27">1Jn 2:27</reference>.
entries.0b7c85c44ee01ade595b059556e3096dddf6f28b: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen3903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3904" type="x-p"/> Take unto thee sweet spices - The holy perfume was compounded of the following ingredients: Stacte - נטף nataph, supposed to be the same with what was afterwards called the balm of Jericho. Stacte is the gum which spontaneously flows from the tree which produces myrrh. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.30.23">Exo 30:23</reference>. <div eID="gen3904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3905" type="x-p"/> Onycha - שחלת shecheleth, allowed by the best critics to be the unguis odoriferans described by Rumph, which is the external crust of the shell-fish purpura or murex, and is the basis of the principal perfumes made in the East Indies. <div eID="gen3905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3906" type="x-p"/> Galbanum - חלבנה chelbenah, the bubon gummiferum or African ferula; it rises with a ligneous stalk from eight to ten feet, and is garnished with leaves at each joint. The top of the stock is terminated by an umbel of yellow flowers, which are succeeded by oblong channelled seeds, which have a thin membrane or wing on their border. When any part of the plant is broken, there issues out a little thin milk of a cream color. The gummy resinous juice which proceeds from this plant is what is commonly called galbanum, from the chelbench of the Hebrews. <div eID="gen3906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3907" type="x-p"/> Pure frankincense - לבנה זקה lebonah zaccah. Frankincense is supposed to derive its name from frank, free, because of its liberal or ready distribution of its odours. It is a dry resinous substance, in pieces or drops of a pale yellowish white color, has a strong smell, and bitter acrid taste. The tree which produces it is not well known. Dioscorides mentions it as gotten in India. What is called here pure frankincense is no doubt the same with the mascula thura of Virgil, and signifies what is first obtained from the tree - that which is strongest and most free from all adventitious mixtures. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.30.7">Exo 30:7</reference>. <div eID="gen3907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3908" type="x-p"/> The Israelites were most strictly prohibited, on the most awful penalties, from making any anointing oil or perfume similar to those described in this chapter. He that should compound such, or apply any of this to any common purpose, even to smell to, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.38">Exo 30:38</reference>, should be cut off, that is, excommunicated from his people, and so lose all right, title, and interest in the promises of God and the redemption of Israel. From all this we may learn how careful the Divine Being is to preserve his own worship and his own truth, so as to prevent them from being adulterated by human inventions; for he will save men in his own way, and upon his own terms. What are called human inventions in matters of religion, are not only of no worth, but are in general deceptive and ruinous. Arts and sciences in a certain way may be called inventions of men, for the spirit of a man knoweth the things of a man - can comprehend, plan, and execute, under the general influence of God, every thing in which human life is immediately concerned; but religion, as it is the gift, so it is the invention, of God: its doctrines and its ceremonies proceed from his wisdom and goodness, for he alone could devise the plan by which the human race may be restored to his favor and image, and taught to worship him in spirit and in truth. And that worship which himself has prescribed, we may rest assured, will be most pleasing in his sight. Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire before the Lord; and their destruction by the fire of Jehovah is recorded as a lasting warning to all presumptuous worshippers, and to all who attempt to model his religion, according to their own caprice, and to minister in sacred things without that authority which proceeds from himself alone. The imposition of hands whether of pope, cardinal, or bishop can avail nothing here. The call and unction of God alone can qualify the minister of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.  <chapter eID="Exod.30"/> <div eID="gen3908" type="x-p"/>

entries.09977303bcf4c874aa85c7fa100a8b0fbd5c2cbf: <reference osisRef="Exod.30.1-Exod.30.6">Exo 30:1-6</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.37.25-Exod.37.28">Exo 37:25-28</reference>). Moses was directed to make an <hi type="italic">altar of burning of incense</hi> (lit., incensing of incense), of acacia-wood, one cubit long and one broad, four-cornered, two cubits high, furnished with horns like the altar of burnt-offering (<reference osisRef="Exod.27.1-Exod.27.2">Exo 27:1-2</reference>), and to plate it with pure gold, the roof (גּג) thereof (i.e., its upper side or surface, which was also made of wood), and its walls round about, and its horns; so that it was covered with gold quite down to the ground upon which it stood, and for this reason is often called the golden altar (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.38">Exo 39:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.40.5">Exo 40:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.40.26">Exo 40:26</reference>; Num 4:11). Moreover it was to be ornamented with a golden wreath, and furnished with golden rings at the corners for the carrying-poles, as the ark of the covenant and the table of shew-bread were (Exo 25:11., Exo 25:25.); and its place was to be in front of the curtain, which concealed the ark of the covenant (<reference osisRef="Exod.26.31">Exo 26:31</reference>), “before the capporeth” (<reference osisRef="Exod.40.5">Exo 40:5</reference>), so that, although it really stood in the holy place between the candlestick on the south side and the table on the north (<reference osisRef="Exod.26.35">Exo 26:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.40.22">Exo 40:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.40.24">Exo 40:24</reference>), it was placed in the closest relation to the <hi type="italic">capporeth</hi>, and for this reason is not only connected with the most holy place in 1Ki 6:22, but is reckoned in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.4">Heb 9:4</reference> as part of the furniture of the most holy place (see <hi type="italic">Delitzsch</hi> on <reference osisRef="Heb.9.4">Heb 9:4</reference>).
entries.4552f75056aeb56c9474b48cfb5abdc9046a9be9: <reference osisRef="Exod.30.7-Exod.30.9">Exo 30:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen1057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1058" type="x-p"/> Upon this altar Aaron was to burn fragrant incense, the preparation of which is described in Exo 30:34., every morning and evening before Jehovah, at the time when he trimmed the lamps. No “strange incense” was to be offered upon it, - i.e., incense which Jehovah had not appointed (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.10.1">Lev 10:1</reference>), that is to say, which had not been prepared according to His instructions-nor burnt sacrifice, nor meat-offering; and no drink-offering was to be poured upon it. As the altar of incense was not only marked as a place of sacrifice by its name מזבּח, “place of slain-offering,” but was put on a par with the altar of sacrifice by its square shape and its horns, it was important to describe minutely what sacrifices were to be offered upon it. For the burning of fragrant incense is shown to be a sacrifice, by the fact that it was offered upon a place of sacrifice, or altar. Moreover the word הקטיר, to cause to ascend in smoke and steam, from קטר to smoke or steam, is not only applied to the lighting of incense, but also to the lighting and burning of the bleeding and bloodless sacrifices upon the altar of incense. Lastly, the connection between the incense-offering and the burnt-offering is indicated by the rule that they were to be offered at the same time. Both offerings shadowed forth the devotion of Israel to its God, whilst the fact that they were offered every day exhibited this devotion as constant and uninterrupted. But the distinction between them consisted in this, that in the burnt or whole offering Israel consecrated and sanctified its whole life and action in both body and soul to the Lord, whilst in the incense-offering its prayer was embodied as the exaltation of the spiritual man to God (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.8">Rev 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.3-Rev.8.4">Rev 8:3-4</reference>); and with this there was associated the still further distinction, that the devotion was completed in the burnt-offering solely upon the basis of the atoning sprinkling of blood, whereas the incense-offering presupposed reconciliation with God, and on the basis of this the soul rose to God in this embodiment of its prayer, and was thus absorbed into His Spirit. In this respect, the incense-offering was not only a spiritualizing and transfiguring of the burnt-offering, but a completion of that offering also.
entries.409111f4711688d8982f10a2b3158eee685d4bcb: <reference osisRef="Exod.30.10">Exo 30:10</reference> <div eID="gen1058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1059" type="x-p"/> Once a year Aaron was to expiate the altar of incense with the blood of the sin-offering of atonement, because it was most holy to the Lord, that is to say, as is expressly observed in the directions concerning this expiatory act (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.18-Lev.16.19">Lev 16:18-19</reference>), to purify it from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel. כּפּר, with על <hi type="italic">objecti constr.</hi>, signifies literally to cover over a thing, then to cover over sin, or make expiation. In the second clause we have “<hi type="italic">upon it</hi>” (the altar) instead of “upon the horns of it,” because the altar itself was expiated in its horns. The use of מן in מדּם is to be explained on the ground that only a part of the blood of the sin-offering was smeared with the finger upon the horns. (For further remarks, see at <reference osisRef="Lev.16.18">Lev 16:18</reference>-19.) The term “most holy” is not only applied to this altar, in common with the inner division of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Exod.26.33">Exo 26:33</reference>), but also to the altar of burnt-offering (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.37">Exo 29:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.40.10">Exo 40:10</reference>), and all the vessels of the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.29">Exo 30:29</reference>), which were anointed with holy oil; then to the whole of the tabernacle in its holiest aspect (Num 18:10); and lastly, to all the sacrifices, which were given up entirely to Jehovah (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.2.3">Lev 2:3</reference>); - consequently to everything which stood in so intimate a relation to Jehovah as to be altogether removed, not only from use and enjoyment on the part of man, but also from contact on the part of unsanctified men. Whoever touched a most holy thing was sanctified thereby (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.30.29">Exo 30:29</reference> with <reference osisRef="Exod.29.37">Exo 29:37</reference>). <div eID="gen1059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1060" type="x-p"/> The Atonement-Money, which every Israelite had to pay at the numbering of the people, has the first place among the supplementary instructions concerning the erection and furnishing of the sanctuary, and serves to complete the demand for freewill-offerings for the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.1-Exod.25.9">Exo 25:1-9</reference>).
entries.222d4c7b7f9333829fbdee01234af10385f16bf6: <reference osisRef="Exod.30.12-Exod.30.15">Exo 30:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen1060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1061" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel according to them that are numbered, they shall give every one an expiation for his soul to the Lord at their numbering, that a plague may not strike them</hi> (happen to them) <hi type="italic">at their numbering</hi>.” פּקד, lit., adspexit, then inspexit explorandi causa, hence to review, or number an army or a nation, for the purpose of enrolling for military service. לפקדיהם with reference to the numbered, <hi type="italic">qui in censum veniunt</hi>. כּפר (expiation, expiation-money, from כּפּר to expiate) is to be traced to the idea that the object for which expiation was made was thereby withdrawn from the view of the person to be won or reconciled. It is applied in two ways: (1) on the supposition that the face of the person to be won was covered by the gift (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.21">Gen 32:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3">1Sa 12:3</reference>); and (2) on the supposition that the guilt itself was covered up (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>), or wiped away (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.23">Jer 18:23</reference>), so far as the eye of God was concerned, as though it had no longer any existence, and that the sinful man was protected from the punishment of the judge in consequence of this covering. In this way כּפר has acquired the meaning λύτρον, a payment by which the guilty are redeemed (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.30">Exo 21:30</reference>; Num 35:31); and this is the meaning which it has in the passage before us, where the soul is said to be protected by the <hi type="italic">copher</hi>, so as to be able to come without danger into the presence of the holy God (Num 8:19. See <hi type="italic">Oehler</hi> in <hi type="italic">Herzog's</hi> Cycl.). Such an approach to God took place at the numbering of the people for the purpose of enrolling them in the army of Jehovah (Num 1:3, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.7.4">Exo 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Exo 12:41</reference>). Hence “every one who passed over to those that were numbered,” who was enrolled among them, i.e., in the army of Jehovah, - that is to say, every male Israelite of 20 years old and upwards (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.14">Exo 30:14</reference>), - was to pay half a shekel of the sanctuary as atonement-money; the rich no more, the poor no less (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.15">Exo 30:15</reference>), because all were equal in the sight of Jehovah; and this payment was to be a “heave” (<hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, see <reference osisRef="Exod.25.2">Exo 25:2</reference>) for Jehovah for the expiation of the souls. The shekel of the sanctuary, which contained 20 gerahs, was no doubt the original shekel of full weight, as distinguished from the lighter shekel which was current in ordinary use. In <reference osisRef="Exod.38.26">Exo 38:26</reference> the half shekel is called בּקע, lit., the split, i.e., half, from בּקע to split; and we find it mentioned as early as the time of the patriarchs as a weight in common use for valuing gold (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.22">Gen 24:22</reference>), so that, no doubt, even at that time there were distinct silver pieces of this weight, which were probably called shekels when employed for purposes of trade, since the word <hi type="italic">shekel</hi> itself does not denote any particular weight, as we may perceive at once form a comparison of 1Ki 10:17 and <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.16">2Ch 9:16</reference>, at least so far as later times are concerned. The sacred shekel, to judge from the weight of Maccabean shekels, which are in existence still, and vary from 256 to 272 Parisian grains, weighed 274 grains, and therefore, according to present valuation, would be worth 26 groschen (about 2s. 7d.), so that the half-shekel of bekah would be 13 groschen (1s. 3 1/2d.).
entries.4cda7bac4335f40897305fdcd61da201398ab1da: <reference osisRef="Exod.30.16">Exo 30:16</reference> <div eID="gen1061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1062" type="x-p"/> This atonement-money Moses was to appropriate to the work of the sanctuary (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.38.25-Exod.38.28">Exo 38:25-28</reference>, where the amount and appropriation are reported). Through this appropriation it became “<hi type="italic">a memorial to the children of Israel before the Lord to expiate their souls,</hi>” i.e., a permanent reminder of their expiation before the Lord, who would henceforth treat them as reconciled because of this payment. It was no ordinary tribute, therefore, which Israel was to pay to Jehovah as its King, but an act demanded by the holiness of the theocratic covenant. As an expiation for souls, it pointed to the unholiness of Israel’s nature, and reminded the people continually, that by nature it was alienated from God, and could only remain in covenant with the Lord and live in His kingdom on the ground of His grace, which covered its sin. It was not till this sinful nature had been sanctified by a perfect atonement, and servitude under the law had been glorified and fully transformed into that sonship to which Israel was called as the first-born son of Jehovah, that as children of the kingdom they had no longer to pay this atonement-money for their souls (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.25-Matt.17.26">Mat 17:25-26</reference>). - According to Num 1:1, Num 1:18, as compared with <reference osisRef="Exod.40.17">Exo 40:17</reference>, the census of the nation was not taken till a month after the building of the tabernacle was completed, and yet the atonement-money to be paid at the taking of the census was to be appropriated to the purpose of the building, and must therefore have been paid before. This apparent discrepancy may be reconciled by the simple assumption, that immediately after the command of God had been issued respecting the building of the tabernacle and the contributions which the people were to make for the purpose, the numbering of the males was commenced and the atonement-money collected from the different individuals, that the tabernacle was then built and the whole ceremonial instituted, and that, after all this had been done, the whole nation was enrolled according to its tribes, fathers’ houses, and families, on the basis of this provisional numbering, and thus the census was completed. For this reason the census gave exactly the same number of males as the numbering (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.38.26">Exo 38:26</reference> and Num 1:46), although the one had been carried out nine months before the other.
entries.320ee929707a2e3a8d715ca3cdccb5472bcb9a55: <reference osisRef="Exod.30.17-Exod.30.21">Exo 30:17-21</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.38.8">Exo 38:8</reference>). The Brazen Laver, and its use. - The making of this vessel is not only mentioned in a supplementary manner, but no description is given of it because of the subordinate position which it occupied, and from the fact that it was not directly connected with the sanctuary, but was only used by the priests to cleanse themselves for the performance of their duties. כּיּור: a basin, a round, caldron-shaped vessel. כּגּו (its support): by this we are not to understand the pedestal of the caldron, but something separate from the basin, which was no doubt used for drawing off as much water as was required for washing the officiating priests. For although כּן belongs to כּיּור, the fact that it is always specially mentioned in connection with the basin necessarily leads to the conclusion, that it had a certain kind of independence (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.31.9">Exo 31:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.35.16">Exo 35:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.39.39">Exo 39:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.40.11">Exo 40:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.8.11">Lev 8:11</reference>). These two vessels were to be made of brass or copper, like the other things in the court; and, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.38.8">Exo 38:8</reference>, they were made of the brass of the mirrors of the women who served before the door of the tabernacle. הצּבאת בּמראת does not mean either “provided with mirrors of the women” (Bähr, i. pp. 485-6), or ornamented “with forms, figures of women, as they were accustomed to appear at the sanctuary” (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). But these views are overthrown by the fact, that ב never signifies with in the sense of an outward addition, but always denotes the means, “not an independent object, but something accompanying and contributing to the action referred to” (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §217, <hi type="italic">f</hi>. 3). In this case ב can only apply to the material used, whether we connect it with ויּעשׂ as in <reference osisRef="Exod.31.4">Exo 31:4</reference>, or, what seems decidedly more correct, with נחשׁת as a more precise definition; so that ב would denote that particular quality which distinguished the brass of which the basin was made (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §217 <hi type="italic">f</hi>.), - apart altogether from the fact, that neither the mirrors of women, nor the figures of women, would form a fitting ornament for the basin, as the priests did not require to look at themselves when they washed their hands and feet; and there is still less ground for <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> fiction, that Levitical women went to the sanctuary at particular times, forming a certain procession, and taking things with them for the purpose of washing, cleaning, and polishing. The true meaning is given by the Septuagint, ἐκ τῶν κατόπτρων. According to <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.22">1Sa 2:22</reference>, the צבאת were women, though not washer-women, but women who dedicated their lives to the service of Jehovah, and spent them in religious exercises, in fasting and in prayer, like Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, mentioned in Luk 2:37.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> objection to this explanation, viz., that “at a time when the sanctuary was not yet erected, the author could not speak of women as coming to the door of the sanctuary, or performing religious service there,” would contain its own refutation, if there were any ground for it at all. For before the sanctuary was erected, the author could not speak of Levitical women as coming at particular times to the sanctuary, and bringing things with them for the purpose of washing and cleaning. But the participle צבאת does not imply that they had served there before the erection of the sanctuary, but only that from that time forward, they did perform service there.</note> צבא denotes spiritual warfare, and is accordingly rendered by the lxx νηστεύειν, by <hi type="italic">Onkelos</hi>, <hi type="italic">orare</hi>, with which the Rabbins agree. The mirrors of the women had been used for the purpose of earthly adorning. But now the pious Israelites renounced this earthly adorning, and offered it to the Lord as a heave-offering to make the purifying laver in front of the sanctuary, in order that “what had hitherto served as a means of procuring applause in the world might henceforth be the means of procuring the approbation of God” (Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Dissert</hi>. vol. ii.). - The laver was to be placed between the tabernacle, i.e., the dwelling, and the altar in the court (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.18">Exo 30:18</reference>), probably not in a straight line with the door of the dwelling and the altar of burnt-offering, but more sideways, so as to be convenient for the use of the priests, whether they were going into the tabernacle, or going up to the altar for service, to kindle a firing for Jehovah, i.e., to offer sacrifice upon the altar. They were to wash their hands, with which they touched the holy things, and their feet, with which they trod the holy ground (see <reference osisRef="Exod.3.5">Exo 3:5</reference>), “that they might not die,” as is again emphatically stated in <reference osisRef="Exod.30.20">Exo 30:20</reference> and Exo 30:21. For touching holy things with unclean hands, and treading upon the floor of the sanctuary with dirty feet, would have been a sin against Jehovah, the Holy One of Israel, deserving of death. These directions do not imply “that, notwithstanding all their consecration, they were regarded as still defiled by natural uncleanness” (<hi type="italic">Baumgarten</hi>), but rather that consecration did not stamp them with a <hi type="italic">character indelebilis</hi>, or protect them from the impurities of the sinful nation in the midst of which they lived, or of their own nature, which was still affected with mortal corruption and sin.
entries.4390c2ee61dcc320843089dc2b88fa765bcc0a23: <reference osisRef="Exod.30.22-Exod.30.25">Exo 30:22-25</reference> <div eID="gen1062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1063" type="x-p"/> The Holy Anointing Oil. - This was to be prepared from the best perfumes ראשׁע בּשׂמים, where ראשׁע, <hi type="italic">caput</hi>, the principal or chief, is subordinate to בּשׂמים), viz., of four fragrant spices and olive-oil. The spices were, (1) liquid myrrh, as distinguished from the dry gum; - (2) קנּמן־בּשׂם, <hi type="italic">cinnamon of fragrance</hi>, the name having been introduced to the Semitic nations along with the thing itself, and then by the Phoenicians to the Greeks and Romans (κίνναμον, <hi type="italic">cinnamum</hi>): whether it came from Ceylon, the great mart of cinnamon, is very doubtful, as there is not word that can be discovered in the Indian dialects corresponding to <hi type="italic">cinnamon</hi>; - (3) <hi type="italic">cane of fragrance</hi>, the κάλαμος ἀρωματικός, <hi type="italic">calamus odoratus</hi>, of the Greek sand Romans, i.e., the scented calamus which is imported from India; - and (4) <hi type="italic">kiddah</hi>, probably <hi type="italic">cassia</hi>, and possibly the species called κιττώ in Dioscor. 1, 12, in which case קציעה (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">Psa 45:9</reference>) is either the generic name for cassia, or else refers to a different species. The proportion in which these spices were to be taken was 500 shekels or 14 1/2 lbs. of myrrh, half the quantity, i.e., 7 lbs, of cinnamon, and the same of calamus and cassia; in all, therefore, 21 lbs. of dry spices, which were to be mixed with one hin of oil (about 5 quarts) and 14 lbs. of liquid myrrh. These proportions preclude the supposition, that the spices were pulverized and mixed with the oil and myrrh in their natural condition, for the result in that case would have been a thick mess: they rather favour the statement of the Rabbins, that the dry spices were softened in water and boiled, to extract their essence, which was then mixed with oil and myrrh, and boiled again until all the watery part had evaporated. An artificial production of this kind is also indicated by the expressions מרקחת רקח “<hi type="italic">spice-work of spice-mixture</hi>,” and רקח מעשׂה “<hi type="italic">labour</hi> (work) <hi type="italic">of the perfumer or ointment-maker</hi>.”
entries.30d7a8d0cbcabd22a6798e1355180b22f5cf2b99: <reference osisRef="Exod.30.26-Exod.30.33">Exo 30:26-33</reference> (see at Lev 8:10.).
